lead.hed: France's next nuclear aircraft carrier will be named for an idea rather than a place or a person, a new USNI News piece reports, tracing the name Liberté back to the Free French naval forces Charles de Gaulle rallied from exile in London after the 1940 fall of France
lead.insight: USNI News' PARIS dispatch opens with the carrier's namesake: pushed from the continent by the Nazi occupation in 1940, Charles de Gaulle established a government in exile in London while a ragtag fleet of French ships carried on fighting as France Libre -- Free France. The piece frames the 80,000-ton successor to the current carrier FS Charles de Gaulle (R91) as carrying that same idea of liberty forward into its name. news.usni.org 403'd (Cloudflare 'Just a moment' challenge) on same-turn fetch, consistent with every news.usni.org attempt this session, so detail beyond this opening passage -- displacement, propulsion, timeline, air wing -- is not available this turn and is not invented here.

lead.image_note: Hero depicts the current carrier FS Charles de Gaulle, the ship this story's successor will replace -- no official photo exists yet of the unbuilt successor carrier. Disclosed here, not on the public page.

political.hed: A Victorian-era British ambassador to Washington who wrote the industrial-age successor to Tocqueville's Democracy in America offers an unsettling lens on this month's midterm result, a new essay argues -- warning that demagoguery and a decayed public opinion, not any single law, are what let democracies rot
political.insight: Providence turns to James Bryce, the Belfast-born scholar-diplomat who served as British ambassador to Washington under Teddy Roosevelt and authored The American Commonwealth, to read the 2026 midterms. Bryce defined healthy democracy as citizens exercising civic responsibility rather than class or partisan interest, and warned that demagogues -- whom he saw in both Conservative leader Benjamin Disraeli and his own Liberal colleagues Gladstone and Lloyd George -- thrive on "indolence, private self-interest, and party spirit" and refashion those vices into democratic virtues. Bryce trusted an educated public opinion, built on universities, public education and a vibrant print culture, to check demagoguery; the essay argues that infrastructure has since decayed, leaving America's 2024 Trump "realignment" reversed just two years later the way Gladstone's Irish Home Rule push ultimately cost his own Liberal Party decades of dominance. It closes pointing to campus "civics centers" in Texas, Florida and Ohio, and to Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's pledge to reinvest in public schools, as rare grounds for optimism.

political.hed: American Federation of Teachers president Randi Weingarten collected $546,158 in total compensation last year even as a book-promotion operation tied to her union keeps expanding, a new commentary finds, with the union's own financial disclosure supplying the pay figure
political.insight: Heritage Foundation's commentary opens by contrasting the modest pay of a classroom teacher with the compensation of a teachers'-union president, citing AFT's own latest financial disclosure to put Weingarten's total compensation at $546,158 last year. heritage.org returned a Cloudflare challenge on same-turn fetch, consistent with every heritage.org attempt this session, so this item relies on the authorized RSS headline and summary only -- the piece's "sleazy book scam" framing and the claim that teachers paid for it are stated beyond this point and not elaborated here.

political.hed: Christians who want real influence in American politics and culture need to stop accepting media-crafted narratives about which believers count as acceptable, a new essay argues, pointing to the elevation of former NIH director Francis Collins as the model evangelical the press is comfortable with
political.insight: American Reformer's essay argues the media and cultural ecosystem is "determined to discourage any intelligent evangelical who shows even the slightest impulse to upset the current regime," and holds up Francis Collins -- the guitar-playing former NIH director who presided over the COVID-19 response and publicly celebrated Pride Month -- as the press's preferred image of an acceptable public evangelical. The fetch stopped at that point (short post or subscriber wall), so this item's insight is limited to that opening argument; the headline, "Lessons from the Huang Affair," points toward a broader argument connecting this narrative pattern to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's recent controversy, but no further detail beyond the fetched paragraph is available this turn.

culture.hed: A new Fox Nation Christian dating reality show styles itself as a wholesome alternative to The Bachelor, complete with Bible studies and prayer circles, but a review finds it opens on its bachelor's shirtless shower scene and runs the same one-man-many-women format underneath the crosses
culture.insight: WORLD's review of "The Vow" -- hosted by Chris Harrison, who spent 19 years fronting ABC's The Bachelor -- follows bachelor Jace Cates, 30, as ten Christian women compete for him across six episodes, with Harrison opening by promising "no roses, no elimination ceremonies, no gimmicks." The review finds the show still leans on Bachelor-style heartbreak and stylish updos and expensive dresses even as contestants read Bibles at men's small groups, form prayer circles after breakups, and sit for interviews with crosses visibly hung in the background. Its verdict: "it's polyamory in pretty packaging," a hard sell for its intended evangelical audience no matter how many crosses are on set.

culture.hed: College football's transformation into a billion-dollar, NIL-and-transfer-portal free market has corroded the sport's character-forming purpose, a new essay argues, and no government agency, university or NCAA fix is likely to put it back together
culture.insight: Law & Liberty's essay, responding to a piece on federal regulation of college sports, argues money has become what sociologist Robert Nisbet called a "cash nexus" that dissolves the loyalty, place-attachment and "sacred" character-forming purpose athletics once carried, turning players into what Nisbet termed "loose individuals" free to transfer for the highest bidder. It cites the University of Michigan paying $7.14 million to its athletic director not to work there, $10 million to its fired offensive coordinator, a likely $25 million buyout to keep head coach Kyle Whittingham, and a possible $17.2 million buyout for an AD who never occupied the chair, alongside the O'Bannon case that opened the door to paying players for name and likeness. Drawing on Johan Huizinga's Homo Ludens, the essay argues sport has become "profane" once play lost its ritual, noncommercial character, and closes warning that online sports gambling -- where "covering the spread" now matters more than winning -- is deepening the rot with no fix in sight.

culture.hed: A new book drawn from Pope Francis' private diaries reveals a man consumed by fear of what he called his own "temptation to omnipotence" and a conviction that "mercy is my real story," a Dominican theologian writes in a review that reconsiders a pontificate he often struggled to defend
culture.insight: First Things' review of Cardinal Víctor Fernández's "The Private Diary of Pope Francis" is written by a Dominican priest and theologian who says he frequently defended Francis's statements to fellow Catholics while privately wishing the pope hadn't made the defense so difficult. The diary entries, kept intermittently from 1992 to August 2024, show Francis returning repeatedly to Ezekiel 16 on divine mercy toward an unfaithful Jerusalem, and naming his episcopal motto miserando atque eligendo as an expression of "mercy is my real story." The most revealing passages concern what Francis called his life's great spiritual temptation -- "the temptation to omnipotence," manifesting as an inability to say no, distrust of others and a drift toward manipulating people -- including an acknowledged period of intense spiritual trial in 2021-2022. The reviewer, who has held senior posts in his own order, closes by applying to Francis the same principle Francis preached: that a person should not be reduced to his failures.
